Hi [~accountid:5cd561c3d210950fd02d1b51] - thanks for flagging this. I include my comments below.

----

h3. +*Issue 1: Requirement not to upload ‘sensitive’ data.*+

As a preliminary comment, I should clarify exactly what I mean here when I say “sensitive” data. In practical terms, this is the following:

* The categories of data explicitly listed in Clause 7(b): *Health info*, *social security numbers*, and *bank account/payment/credit card info*.
* The categories of data defined as ‘special category’ in the GDPR: Personal data revealing *racial or ethnic origin*, *political opinions*, *religious/philosophical beliefs*,  *trade union membership*, *genetic data*, *biometric data*, *health data* or data concerning *sex life/sexual orientation*.
* Additional categories considered as ‘sensitive’ under the GDPR: Personal data relating to *criminal convictions/offences*, or *children’s data*.

At present (i.e., if we do not amend the Agreement), if we include such categories of information in the docs / files that we upload, then we may be in breach. This will not be practical for us - particularly as you mention that in the future we may upload details of injuries sustained (which arguably is health data, and so could put us in breach! (!)). This is why we need to be extra careful with the info we provide.

In terms of how to address this issue, we need to take a two-pronged approach:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# Implement {color:#4c9aff}*internal guidance / processes*{color} to ensure that the Bolt POCs responsible for uploading the docs / files know not to include any of the above categories of data in the documents that they upload (as you suggested). 
## Where a document does contain these categories of info, the info should be redacted first.
## Such guidance / processes should also contain recommendations to not contain unnecessary personal data about Bolt users (e.g., drivers, as you mentioned) - although not prohibited under the Agreement, this is generally important for data minimisation purposes.
# Push for {color:#4c9aff}*less stringent (or none at all) restrictions in the Agreement*{color} regarding uploading sensitive data (as it is likely that edge cases will still slip through the net, even with guidance / processes). 
## This is what I am currently pushing for as part of negotiations with LG.
{panel}

----

h3. +*Issue 2: Categories of ‘Customer Data’ to list in the Agreement*+

I fully appreciate that we will not be able to list every category of personal data that may be included in the docs that we upload - this would not be feasible. Nevertheless, the list you have provided is very useful, so thank you 🙏 

In terms of how to update the text that we previously discussed, I would recommend the following (see green text) (i) This includes the categories of personal data you have listed, while also leaving the floor open for anything else that slips through the net.

{quote}*_“In relation to Customer Data:_*  _LogicGate does not as a matter of course review Customer Data to determine if it contains Personal Data. Customer intends to export the following categories of Personal Information:_ {color:#36b37e}_Names, contact information, title, authorship information (including tags, approvals and attestations), and any other Personal Data forming part of Customer Data provided by the Customer during the term of the Agreement_{color}”{quote}

Hi [~accountid:712020:a335a5ec-2969-45be-8f2f-6561cf7e7d62] ,

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Following deeper research, it seems that our current practice of requiring criminal background checks from employees in Estonia is *not compliant with Estonian law*. This covers both initial hiring and repeat checks (e.g., every three years).
{panel}

h3. What Estonian law allows

Criminal background checks are only permitted in very narrow cases:

# *Working with children* – mandatory checks with annual renewal.
# *Vital Service Providers (VSPs)* under the Emergency Act (utilities, payments, etc.). Based on our understanding, Bolt is not classified as a VSP.
# *Direct cash-handling roles* – and even then, the employer may only ask a *single yes/no question* about current property-related convictions. Employers cannot demand a full extract; this is a strict data-minimisation carve-out.

In all other cases, requiring criminal-record extracts or periodic refreshes is unlawful in Estonia.

h3. Next steps and open questions

# Please confirm the *background and rationale* for collecting criminal background information.
# Was this set up as a global standard procedure, not adapted to Estonia?

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
On our end, we would like to double-confirm our findings with external counsel before advising a formal change, but in the meantime we would like to assess how disruptive (or not) updating the procedure for Estonia would be.

Please do not consider this advice to be final.
{panel}

h3. Internal research note – sources used (with links)

# **[Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate (AKI) Employment FAQ|https://www.aki.ee/isikuandmed/kkk/toosuhted#tsuhted-2]:** This clarifies that employers cannot require extracts from employees and that consent is generally not valid in the employment context.
# **Criminal Records Database Act (Karistusregistri seadus) – §16:** This prohibits demanding criminal record data directly from individuals.
# **Emergency Act (Hädaolukorra seadus):** As of October 18, 2024, this imposes background-check obligations only for Vital Service Providers (we understand Bolt is not classified as such).
# **Sotsiaalkindlustusamet guidance:** This prescribes mandatory annual checks for employees working with children.

When using a 10 minute timeframe, the “model used vs unused metric at order placement” has a high variance, probably due to low volumes during the night. Adding an alert to identify faulty releases would trigger a lot of fault positives.

!image-20250926-070943.png|width=1382,height=795,alt="image-20250926-070943.png"!

In contrast, when using a 1-day timeframe the metric becomes quite stable. However, an alert which uses this time frame will not be useful to timely detect faulty releases.

!image-20250926-072516.png|width=1856,height=835,alt="image-20250926-072516.png"!

Decided to use the 1d timeframe for the alert. This would serve two purposes:

* trigger in case of a faulty release (probably too late to rollback, but at least we have a starting point).
* trigger in case of decaying coverage - either due to new cities launched or area expansion

Will use a 40% threshold for starters.

Current setup proposal:

A donation of up to C$20K to the FYFB is made by Hopp comprised of

* A booking fee added to a charity category of $1 per trip that riders would pay *[<< this needs to be legally a fee paid to Hopp, and looking from the charity side, it will be Hopp (not the passenger) making the $1 donation to the charity out of Hopp own funds]*
* Hopp matches the $1 for every trip up to $10K for a total of up to $20K [<< this is an additional $1 by Hopp to the previous $1 by Hopp]

At the moment reading the T&Cs and the contract signed with FYFB, it actually looks like the set up is category “red”: ” 🔴We mediate donation payment from passenger to charity.” 

# The T&Cs say that passenger makes a donation and _“this $1.00 will then be donated in full to the Project”_.  For comparison, in the UK Bike Project T&Cs: _“On completion of your ride, this 50p will then be donated by Bolt,_ *_using its own funds_*_, to the Project, to assist its mission of making mobility more accessible to the United Kingdom’s refugee community.”_
# The agreement signed with FYFB states that Hopp will “remit” the donations made by riders. << This implies that Hopp mediates passenger’s donation payment to charity, which we want to avoid.

*How to fix this?*

* Let’s amend the T&Cs to clearly reflect that the passenger pays the amount +to Hopp+, Hopp donates +out of its own funds+. We could rely more on the wording of the UK Bike Project T&Cs, e.g. “_Hopp,_ *_using its own funds”_* or similar language. ([ |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rBXWSDUyAquNiXXHXAjr5v203gnbGw2i5W7242ynpEY/edit?tab=t.0][+The Bike Project, Bolt’s Terms and Conditions+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rBXWSDUyAquNiXXHXAjr5v203gnbGw2i5W7242ynpEY/edit?tab=t.0] (UK) )
* Can we also amend the already signed agreement with FYFB? The contract with FYFB (Clause 3 “Donations and matching”) should make clear that it is not that Hopp mediates (“remits”) donation payments from customers to charity but legally speaking Hopp makes the donations. Will be happy to review wording, if needed.
* [+Kerli Uibo+|mailto:kerli.uibo@bolt.eu] How do we treat the amount which the passenger pays to Hopp? Can you confirm that this amount/fee paid by the passenger will be treated as paid by passenger to Hopp, i.e. when the passenger has made payment, the $1.00 will be Hopp money/revenue? And the payment which Hopp makes to the charity is made out of Hopp own funds?

Sorry for getting ahead of myself. I was just trying to state my worries in advance to avoid reaching only a temporary or short-term solution.

I am unsure which exact access is causing the issue. However, from our comparison of the permissions for our in-house agent role and the outsourced agent’s role, it appears that this rides-related access could be the key.

Our team has worked as Delivery CS for many years, and we are well aware of the basic process of changing the phone number of a delivery partner. But the issue we are trying to address here prevents the outsourced agents from handling such trivial requests this way.

For the sake of clarity, let’s take the partner profile you shared - Radek Pavlík. If this profile was affected by this issue we are encountering, you/we would also be able to find another inactive profile with the same phone number in the admin. And this inactive profile would have the _Phone confirmed_ checkbox ticked, which seems to be preventing the change of phone number in the main active profile. The inactive profile also has “x” letters filled in the _First name_ and _Surname_ cells. We found out, that once an in-house agent finds the inactive profile and unticks the _Phone confirmed_ checkbox, then the phone number can be easily changed in the main profile - following the process you shared. But the outsourced agents are unable to find the inactive “x x” profiles. Likely because these profiles are not considered delivery-related. 

In the Beehive case, which Nikola stated while creating this SD ticket, you can see the exact above-described scenario in practice:

* [*_Beehive ticket_*|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/646784330] where the delivery partner requested their phone number change.
* [*_Partners page_*|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet-root/partners?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22phone%22%3A%22%2B420722692457%22%2C%22show_totals%22%3Afalse%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FPrague] of the admin, when we look up their phone number.
** Notice the other account with “x x” instead of the name.
*** The _Phone Confirmed_ was ticked in this profile and only once we unticked it, it was possible to change the phone number in the main profile.

I assume the inactive profiles could be caused by unfinished sign-up processes, if the delivery partner filled the sign-up form multiple times but only finished once. Or that it could have been a case of phone number recycling. But there could be other causes, which I am unaware of.

[~accountid:712020:ca818823-efac-45fe-ba7d-a6686a5e08b5] I understand why this initiative may have been approved last year in Germany. However, in the present case I see several risks that should be flagged for discussion and assessment.

# *Branding / reputational risk*

* The term _“Formula”_ has strong associations with racing and speed, which may be perceived as incentivising unsafe driving practices.
* Even with disclaimers, critics could argue that the name implicitly encourages drivers to compete on speed, creating reputational and potential liability exposure. If a Bolt driver crashes and someone connects it to “Formula Bolt,” we’re exposed reputationally.
* Maybe we can consider rebranding away from _“Formula”_ (e.g. _“Bolt League”_, _“Bolt Cup”_) to avoid racing connotations.

# *Legal/contractual framework in Nordic FO markets*

* In Nordic countries, I think that drivers are typically employed by fleet owners (FOs), right?
* Automatic enrolment of drivers and direct prize distribution from Bolt to drivers could be seen as Bolt circumventing the FO–driver contractual relationship, undermining FO independence, and strengthening arguments for driver reclassification as Bolt’s employees.
* *Proposed mitigation*:
** Secure prior FO agreement that (i) each driver may individually decide whether to participate in this campaign, (ii) both FO and driver (or driver only) are informed of participation, T&C and other comms, and (iii) FO consents to prizes being paid directly to the driver.
** Alternatively, if Nordic is primarily an FO market, we can structure the competition so that FOs (not individual drivers) are the formal participants, with prizes allocated at FO level. I’m not entirely sure this would achieve Bolt’s goals, but maybe?

# *T&Cs*

* Nordic prize promotion regulations require transparent and fair conditions to prevent disputes or challenges.
* T&Cs must clearly set out: eligibility criteria, enrolment/opt-out process, tie-breaker rules, exclusions, and prize distribution mechanisms.
* So Bolt should draft and review tailored T&Cs ensuring compliance with EU and Nordic promotional law.

# *Reclass risk*

The “Formula Bolt” campaign, with automatic driver enrollment, direct communications, and a leaderboard where Bolt evaluates and rewards driver behavior based on defined KPIs, could be seen as a *marker of employment status*. This is especially sensitive in Sweden and Norway, where unions and regulators are actively seeking evidence that platforms effectively control drivers. It can be argued that the setup resembles employer control (monitoring, disciplinary measures, bonus systems), which would strengthen reclassification arguments.

The risk is somewhat lower when drivers operate under FO, since the FO is the formal employer. However, if Bolt communicates directly with drivers, enrolls them automatically, or pays prizes straight to individuals, it undermines the FO structure and brings the reclassification risk back.

Trying to reduce exposure, we could:

* *Avoid automatic enrollment* and make participation voluntary;
* *Channel communications and enrollment via FOs*, ensuring Bolt is seen as a marketing partner, not a direct manager, or obtain FO approval as provided for in point 2.

[~accountid:712020:7f47c2af-14e1-4206-a795-ac87cb906276], would you have any additional thoughts on how we could avoid the risk related to reclass in this situation? Thanks!

* It is unclear to me whether prizes granted directly to drivers (vs. FOs) may trigger tax withholding obligations, create additional reporting burdens, or otherwise alter the nature of the contractual relationships. So could you[~accountid:712020:8bcb68bd-f8da-4da1-8320-2536f6bb0c0c]please assess potential corporate and individual tax implications of awarding prizes directly to drivers vs. via FOs? Hi [~accountid:712020:ca818823-efac-45fe-ba7d-a6686a5e08b5] - I have reviewed this from the privacy law side and include my comments below.

As a preliminary point, although I appreciate that this previously was green-lit in Germany, *this does not yet mean it has been legally approved for the Nordics* (!) The latter are different countries with different laws and risk profiles for Bolt, and so we (being Privacy Legal and Regional Legal) *still need to review and consider this campaign before we sign off on it*, even if it follows the German model 🔍 This is particularly important given the short review timeline - we don’t want to rush into this on the assumption that its fine, only to later find out that it raises unnecessary local law risks.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*In summary*, my advice from a _privacy law_ POV is as follows:

* *Automatic participation*: Although our preference would be for opt-in, we can proceed with automatically adding all drivers to Formula Bolt *_provided that_* they are easily able to opt out at any time.
* *T&Cs / Comms*: The email drafts look fine from a privacy POV (although they should contain an unsubscribe link, and ideally the participants should be able to opt out at any time rather than by a specific deadline). We still need to prepare T&Cs for this campaign in line with the version used in Germany ([+*link*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1U3SYP2IwXFwj5diPkz00fdqtQHg185ELjl83MGLp1RA/edit?tab=t.0]).
* *Leaderboard IDs*: Our preference would be to use a different unique / made-up identifier for drivers and fleets, rather than their account ID (can you please provide a screenshot example of where drivers can see this in their app?). If possible, we should also only display relevant parts of the Leaderboard to users.
* *Sending prizes to drivers*: From a privacy POV, it is fine to send the gift cards to drivers rather than their fleets (but check this with Regional Legal). Ideally this would be via email, rather than making the driver come into the office, though the latter is also an option.
* *Other points*: We should ensure we are implementing usual common-sense processes such as data minimisation, an appeals process, sensible retention practices and ensuring users can opt-out of receiving the emails.
{panel}

I include further details / context on each of these points below. If you have any Qs then let me know!

----

||*Issue*||*Advice*||*Priority*||
|*Automatic participation*
Fleet owners and drivers may take issue with being automatically enrolled in this campaign, particularly since it tracks their ‘performance’ (i.e., the trips they are completing) and openly compares it to others. This may lead some users to issue complaints to Bolt that either: (a) they should have been asked for opt-in consent; or (b) the opt-out processes were not clear enough.|As previously advised for Germany (see [+LSS-33385+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-33385]), our preference would be to make enrolment into the campaign be on an *_opt-in_* basis - this would be the best way of preventing user complaints on this issue.
However, if the business is prioritising making enrolment on an *automatic* basis (which I assume is the case), *we can do this subject to the following* (/) 
* Opt-out options / links should be *clearly displayed* to users in the comms (and ideally on the landing page / Leadership Board as well); and
* The option to opt-out should not be limited to a specific period - users should be able to opt-out *at any time* (privacy laws give users the right to object to the processing of their personal data at any time - if we limit the exercise of this right to a period of time, we are opening ourselves up to accusations that we are not respecting this right - as such, the comms should ideally not say that users only have a limited window to opt out).|🔴|
|*T&Cs*
We need to ensure that Campaign Terms are implemented (and hyperlinked in the comms) to ensure fairness and limit the prospects of frustrated drivers challenging the results. These T&Cs should also include clear privacy language to explain to users what metrics will be used to measure their performance (see Clause 6 of the draft).|I have not yet seen a draft of the T&Cs (the doc previously provided was comms only) - presumably it would be based on [this draft|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1U3SYP2IwXFwj5diPkz00fdqtQHg185ELjl83MGLp1RA/edit?tab=t.0], but they still *need to be prepared* :loading:

|*Contents of the Leaderboard*
Although it is great that we are pseudonymising the drivers in the Leaderboard, using account IDs to do so raises a few risks. In particular, our usual policy at Bolt is to +*not*+ share internal user identifiers (including account IDs) externally for security purposes (as if a data leak occurred, then malicious actors could use these IDs to cause drivers harm in our systems). For context - we do not even share account IDs in response to driver access requests - they are that confidential. The risks are even more prominent here given that the Leaderboard will be publicly accessible to anyone (i.e., anyone can see a wide range of confidential account IDs).
You mentioned that all drivers can easily see their ID in the app - {color:#4c9aff}*are you sure this is the case*{color}? If so, could you please provide me with a screenshot example? (?)|Although I appreciate it was taken as the approach in Germany, my preference would be to +*not*+ *use account IDs as the identifiers* in the Leaderboard, but to instead use a uniquely-generated identifier for each user (!) Although I appreciate this may result in operational effort, it would save exposing Bolt users (and Bolt itself) to unnecessary security risks).
Also, it would be helpful to understand if there are ways to *limit the ability of anyone to see the entire Leaderboard* at any time - if there is a way to tailor it to the viewer and limit the data being viewed publicly, this would be preferable. For example, could the rows being displayed be limited to just the relevant user and the Top 10? Could it also be limited on a country-by-country basis?|🔴|
|*Providing prizes to the drivers*
From a strictly privacy POV, providing the prizes to the drivers directly (rather than via the fleets) is fine. In terms of _how_ to deliver the prize, the main risk to flag is that if drivers are made to come into the office, presumably they will be asked for a copy of their ID before the prize is handed over - although this is fine in principle, retaining copies of IDs can raise privacy risks.|From a privacy POV, awarding the prizes to the drivers directly is fine - however, definitely check this with Regional Legal, as I am not aware of why the prizes typically go to the fleets first (i.e., there may be a good reason that I am unaware of).
In terms of _how_ to deliver the prizes, email would be easiest and the most preferable approach. If instead the drivers need to collect the prizes from an office, asking for their ID is fine but we should not be keeping a copy.|:green:|
|*Data minimisation*
Since we are ranking drivers by their ‘performance’, disgruntled drivers may try to argue that this is profiling (which carries privacy risks). We can of course argue that it is not, but to make our lives easier, we should ensure that we are only using low risk categories of driver data to calculate their score. |*Appealing system errors*
Since the ranking system is entirely automated, it is possible that it may result in errors, which in turn may infuriate drivers who are close to winning but in the end do not. Additionally, privacy laws restrict our ability to implement fully automated systems which ‘significantly affect’ drivers - although we can argue this does not apply here, an additional means of de-risking this campaign would be to show that drivers that they can challenge a decision if they think there has been an error.|Ideally, we should have a *clearly-defined appeals process* in place, whereby if a system error has occurred then a driver can challenge this and update their score accordingly.
If this will not be operationally feasible, then we can proceed without it as the risk here is ultimately low from a privacy POV.|:green:|
|*Email opt-out*
Since this campaign is promoting incentives to drivers, the comms we are sending can be considered direct marketing. Although we do not require opt-in consent from our users to send them these emails, we must ensure they have a means of opting-out of receiving them at all times.
(Note this is distinct from opting-out of the campaign - this is instead opting-out of receiving the comms)|As is our standard practice, we should ensure that the emails / comms we are sending contain an *unsubscribe link / opt-out mechanism*.|:green:|
|*Retention*
Privacy law requires that we retain personal data only for as long as is necessary. This includes data generated in the context of this campaign.|Once the campaign has finished, we should ideally *purge the campaign data* (i.e., the scores) after a set period of time (e.g., 90 days), unless we need to retain them for specific purposes (e.g., legal / accounting purposes).|:green:|

* Team currently working on a more accurate version of pricing to limit recalculations. Expecting to have ±10% of the orders recalculated as a worst case scenario in V2. 
* Route editor: current set-up - calculation based on _client/lower_ price (no minimum distance rate). Sub-optimal for drivers, would likely push PR recalculated trips outside of the 1 EUR / km regulatory minimum. 
** Needs to be fixed before the V2 version goes live, as confirmed by Buin. V1 likely to stay in test phrase / not rolled out to the user base.

Hi [~accountid:5e6b55b2c54d0a0d044302f1] 
Since there is no clear mechanism for handling this matter, one needs to be introduced:

* It is nowhere stated in the T&Cs that drivers can directly demand the cleaning fee in cash from riders.
* This raises consumer protection concerns — riders are surprised, complain, and may feel extorted. It also creates reputational and legal risk. If drivers collect cash unilaterally, Bolt’s role as the intermediary responsible for collecting payments is undermined.

*Advice:*
Clarify in the driver and rider guidelines and notifications what the correct process is:

* *For drivers:* inform them that they cannot demand cash directly. They must submit evidence of a soiled vehicle through Bolt Support. Bolt will process the claim and reimburse if applicable. How the reimbursement process will work (e.g. deduction from the rider) needs to be discussed with the billing team — I cannot advise on that part.
* *For riders:* remind them that they may be charged a cleaning fee, but drivers cannot demand it in cash. The entire process will be mediated by Bolt if the driver submits a complaint.

To ensure compliance with consumer protection rules, it is important to keep the process transparent and predictable (e.g. by setting pre-defined fee ranges, if possible).

Provided SOC 2 report provides baseline assurance that Cursor has implemented core security controls, but the short period, limited scope, and reliance on AWS/user controls mean it is not strong enough on its own to remove supplier risk concerns.

Findings

# *Short track record*, possible growing pains in security/compliance. We need to revisit supplier and request their next SOC 2 report (covering at least 6–12 months, and ideally broader criteria). 
# The report states that *no significant incidents* occurred during the period. While possibly true, in practice almost all SaaS environments experience at least minor incidents. Lack of transparency may suggest *underreporting* or *immature incident management*. Action item - ask for evidence of *recent incident response tests* and *BC/DR readiness*.
# Scoping issue - the SOC 2 criteria include *Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy*. Cursor’s report only covers *Security*. No assurance on availability (uptime, DR/BCP), confidentiality of data, or processing accuracy, which may be critical depending on your use case.
# *No Testing Exceptions* – Perfect results are unusual; in practice, auditors often note at least minor findings. This could mean controls are new and untested in production scale, or the audit period was too short for issues to emerge.

Pentest report 

Summary

||Area||Assessment||Risk Note||
|*Vulnerability Management*|Moderate|Good responsiveness, but selective fixes raise concern|
|*IAM & Least Privilege*|Weak|Multiple excessive privilege issues|
|*Network Segmentation*|Weak|Public exposure of non-prod DB, lack of Kubernetes policies|
|*Governance / Risk Acceptance*|Weak|“Won’t Fix” on High finding|
|*DevSecOps Maturity*|Improving|Pre-commit hooks added post-fact|
|*Transparency*|Good|Clear CVSS, fixes tracked|

Follow up action items



* *Request a risk acceptance justification* for all “Won’t Fix” items.
* *Ask for compensating controls* (e.g. audit logging, network ACLs, scoped roles).
* *Verify remediation validation evidence* (screenshots, configuration diffs).
* *Review their IAM governance process* — are role templates reviewed and version-controlled?
* *Request evidence on IAM hardening, Kubernetes policy enforcement, and network isolation* in next review.

Hi [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] 

Here is a quick summary of the background and rationale for collecting criminal checks in Estonia:

1) The first formal Background Check Policy was introduced on 19 April 2022, but background checks in Estonia were already conducted before then. The exact pre-2022 conditions are unclear due to staff changes and lack of written records. Since 2022, the list of roles requiring checks has stayed the same.

We follow the [Background Check Policy|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ISO/pages/3850306493/Background+Check+Policy], which (in Section 3) specifies roles subject to checks, mainly positions in financial operations and security, identified as critical due to their responsibilities and risks.

Repeated checks seem to have been an internal practice that continued over time.
- Could you share the source stating this requirement is legally invalid?

2) The current setup and role list originated in Estonia and was later applied globally.
In some countries, including Estonia, candidates or employees must provide their own criminal record extract.

We’re open to reviewing and possibly reducing the number of positions that require checks.

Kind regards,
Aike-Maris

*Key Findings From Expansion Q&A* ([+Link+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/18nGK2w0fdP22MTi7QJlnYAFLIGdVjiNT/edit])
{panel}

* *General:*
** Data Protection Law is now fully harmonised with the GDPR (subject to some minor differences). As such, core requirements are identical (/) 
* *International data transfers:*
** IDPC has not yet published a set of SCCs. However, based on experience, it seems likely that we can rely on the EU SCCS.
** 'Adequate' countries include EU, UK, Switzerland, Canada and USA.
** No specific authorisation is needed from the IDPC to action international data transfers if such transfers are based on an adequacy decision, BCRs or SCCs. However, authorisation is needed if the transfer relies on ad hoc contractual clauses (negotiated between the parties) (!) 
* *Legal bases:*
** There are no legitimate interests that are ‘recognised’ under local law.
** Processing data on criminal convictions and offences is subject to restrictions. Consent alone is not enough - must be expressly authorised by Albanian law, with appropriate safeguards.
* *Marketing*:
** The Instruction governing this was implemented in April 2025, and so has not been formally ‘tested’ yet. As such, although the below are the core points, they may be subject to further interpretation / clarification (!) 
** Soft opt-in can apply to Bolt’s own marketing activities, provided that the data is not sensitive and we have effectively conducted a LIA (/) 
** Soft opt-in can apply to third-party marketing where: (i) the data being processed is limited to name, gender age and address; and (ii) the data subject was informed in advance and did not object (/)  Otherwise, consent is required (!) 
** B2B marketing should generally be out of scope, as direct marketing applies to comms sent to directly identifiable persons. As such, comms sent to generic corporate email addresses should not count (/) 
** If the controller uses profiling (including ‘interest profiles’ for marketing), data subject must be informed about meaningful logic / info involved (!) 
* *High-risk processing*:
** Not yet fully defined by the IDPC (which is still in the process of preparing guidelines on this).
** No additional local requirements regarding processing national ID numbers, ID documents, or biometric data.

# What are some of the core examples of where local law permits the processing of criminal data (which would be relevant to Bolt)? Which law(s) set these out?
# Must we include information on profiling/interest profiles in our privacy notice _regardless_ of whether the processing produces a legal or similarly significant effect?
# Please confirm situation re whether Bolt needs opt-in consent to send third-party marketing.
# What is in-scope for ‘commercial’ comms, and do these always require consent to send via email / SMS?

Please find attached the signed agreement for reference. Bolt’s MRG obligations are included in the following sections:

* Section 5.5: The MRG Period starts from the earlier of:
** actual completion of the branding work; or
** one working day after the vehicle was made available for branding.
* Section 5.6 & 5.7: During the MRG Period:
** Bolt guarantees minimum monthly revenue per Branded Vehicle.
** The guarantee ends when the vehicle is unbranded, removed from the program, or when the cap of €3,000 is reached.
* Section 8: MRG Shortfall is calculated monthly and billed by Hertz.
* Section 11.2: MRG shortfall liability is expressly excluded from the liability cap, highlighting that it's a standalone contractual commitment

 

I understand from your request that you would like to move the MRG from pre-branding to post-branding (car is branded only after the driver picks it up). This affects the point at which the MRG Period starts. If the branding never occurs, the car never becomes a Branded Vehicle, and the MRG does not apply.

 

Essentially, the +*question is*+: *Can Bolt stop making MRG Payments?*

→ I think that yes, Bolt can stop MRG payments prospectively for vehicles that are not branded. Per the contract:

* Only Branded Vehicles trigger the MRG obligation.
* Vehicles that are never branded (i.e., if the branding is skipped or cancelled) never enter an MRG Period.
* Therefore, no MRG payment obligation arises.

However, if a vehicle has already been branded (before or after rental), and notice per section 5.5 was given, then the MRG obligation applies retroactively from that point until unbranding or reaching the cap.

 

+*As you have confirmed that*+ *Hertz is informed and agrees to these changes, next step should be*:

* Proceed with a formal amendment to the Country Addendum (France).
* This should:
** Confirm that branding occurs only post-rental.
** State that no car is deemed branded unless branding is physically completed and notified under Clause 5.5.
** Acknowledge that vehicles not branded will not trigger MRG.

Medbringelse og bruk av cannabis og andre narkotiske stoffer (forbudt etter punkt 4.19.3). •	Krav om å kjøre inn i områder med innkjøringsforbud (stridende mot punkt 4.4 og gjeldende trafikkregler). •	Forsøk på å koble personlige enheter til bilens kontrollsystem (datasikkerhetsrisiko, jf. punkt 3.2.3).

Uakseptabel oppførsel som å legge føtter på armlenet, sette skitne vesker på setene, bruke høyttalersamtaler, og filme med blits inne i bilen (forstyrrende for kjøringen, jf. punkt 4.4).

I hvert tilfelle ble mine korrigerende handlinger fulgt av negative vurderinger fra passasjerene.

Konsekvens •	Stjerneratingen ble redusert på grunn av gjengjeldende vurderinger. •	Automatisk tap av Comfort- og Premium-kategorier uten varsel, jf. punkt 13.5 og 13.6 . •	Ingen mulighet til å identifisere hvilke passasjerer eller turer som ga negative vurderinger, jf. punkt 8.1 (transparens og «gode intensjoner»). •	Eksisterende klagefunksjon pr. tur er ikke effektiv, fordi Bolt ikke opplyser hvilke vurderinger som faktisk utløser degradering.

Juridiske og kontraktsmessige uklarheter •	Pliktkonflikt: Jeg er kontraktsrettslig forpliktet til å håndheve lover og forskrifter, jf. punkt 4.2, men samtidig straffes jeg gjennom rating-systemet når jeg oppfyller denne plikten. •	Manglende transparens: Punkt 8.1 gir Bolt rett til å ignorere vurderinger uten «gode intensjoner». Likevel gis ikke sjåfører informasjon om hvilke vurderinger som ligger til grunn for tap av kategori, hvilket gjør det umulig å bestride eller kontekstualisere dem.

Dette bryter med forordning (EU) 2019/1150 art. 3 og art. 4 om transparens og rett til begrunnelse. •	Klageadgang: Punkt 13.6 gir sjåfører rett til å protestere på suspensjon eller oppsigelse, i tråd med EU-forordningen. Tap av Comfort/Premium-kategorier er en plattformsrestriksjon, og må derfor omfattes av denne retten. •	Ansvarsfraskrivelse: Punkt 12.4 fraskriver Bolt seg ansvar for passasjerers handlinger, men samtidig brukes passasjervurderinger som et sanksjonsverktøy mot sjåfører. Dette er en strukturell inkonsistens som undergraver avtalens integritet.

Anmodning til Bolt Jeg ber om at Bolt: 1.	Opplyser hvilke vurderinger som lå til grunn for degraderingen, og hvordan de er vurdert opp mot kravet i punkt 8.1 om «gode intensjoner». 2.	Bekrefter at tap av Comfort/Premium-kategorier omfattes av klageretten etter punkt 13.6 og forordning (EU) 2019/1150.

_Dear Mr. Spiteri,_

_Thank you for forwarding the complaint submitted by Mr. Michael John Borg. We have carefully reviewed the matter and our internal records, and we provide below our factual account, contractual position, and response in line with Bolt’s passenger terms and conditions and applicable consumer principles._

*_Factual & Payment Background_*

* _We confirm that Mr. Borg scheduled a ride via the Bolt app for 12 September 2025 at_ *_(xxxxx - insert time)_* _to be collected from his residence and transported to the airport._
* _At the time of booking, our system placed a pre-authorisation hold on his payment method. This hold is a verification mechanism, not a charge, and is reversed if no ride is fulfilled._
* _Our payment logs confirm that the hold was released on 12 September at_ *_(xxxxx - insert time)_*_, and no funds were ultimately retained._
* _While Mr. Borg’s complaint refers to multiple attempted bookings (including via his spouse’s account), our system was able to locate only the one scheduled booking under his account. We did not identify any confirmed bookings from the spouse’s account in our logs._
* _The requested ride was broadcast to available drivers within proximity at that hour._
* _No drivers accepted the trip and, as a result, the app returned status messages to Mr. Borg that “no driver available” (or equivalent) rather than a driver cancellation after acceptance._
* _Because no driver accepted the booking, the ride could not proceed, and no contract of carriage was conclusively formed between the passenger and a driver (see 4.1–4.2 of our passenger T&Cs)._

*_Contractual & Terms‑based Position_*

_We refer to the Terms and Conditions for Passengers, available_ [_here_|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/legal/tnc-passengers/?category=rides]_. Key relevant provisions include:_

_Clause 1.1–1.2: The app is a mediation platform; the transport contract is entered between passenger and driver. Bolt does not itself provide transport services._

_Clause 4.1–4.2: A transport service becomes “ordered” only once a driver confirms the request. Until then, the booking is a mediated request, not a guaranteed service._

_Clause 6.1 – 6.2: Bolt disclaims liability for the absence of driver availability and the app cannot guarantee service at all times._

_In light of these provisions, we respectfully submit that we satisfied our contractual obligation to attempt to locate a driver. Because no driver accepted, the transport contract did not crystallize, and we are not liable for reimbursement of consequential costs (e.g. parking, self‑drive, missed flights)._

_We trust this sets out our position clearly. Please let us know if you require further information._

_Yours sincerely,_
